§3 of docs/02-algorithms.md · RFC 7490 · no safe neighbor? tunnel to a safe router further away · code: src/engine/rlfa.ts
Example 2: the ring, protect S–E for E
Every metric is 1. S’s normal path to E is the direct link
(cost 1).
Red dashed: the failed link S–E.
Green arrows: the tunnel S → A → B to PQ node B (one label,
Purple arrows: B takes the packet out and forwards it
normally, B → C → E.
How it works: find routers in both P-space and Q-space
First, no LFA: A fails the loop-free check, 2 < 1 + 1 = 2 is false (A2). So look further
away.
Set Test (strict <) Example 2
P-space of S dist(S,Y) < c(S,E) + dist(E,Y) {A, B}
Extended (via A) dist(A,Y) < dist(A,S) + dist(S,Y) adds C
Q-space of E dist(Y,E) < dist(Y,S) + c(S,E) {B, C}
PQ nodes extended P ∩ Q {B, C}
The numbers
Y P(S): dist(S,Y) < 1 + dist(E,Y) Q(E): dist(Y,E) < dist(Y,S) + 1
Extended via A: dist(A,C) = 2 (A → B → C) < dist(A,S) + dist(S,C) = 1 + 2 = 3 ✓
Which PQ node? (B11: lowest cost from S, then lowest id)
B in plain P(S): dist(S,B) = 2 ← chosen
C only via A: c(S,A) + dist(A,C) = 1 + 2 = 3
Result
S puts the packet in a tunnel to B. B is reached without S–E (P) and reaches E without S–E (Q), so B
just forwards it on its normal table. With Segment Routing the tunnel is B’s Prefix-SID: 16000 + 4 =

Where it fails: Example 3 (B–C = 10)
Same ring, but B–C costs 10, so no shortest path
uses it.
P(S) = {A, B} ext via A: C?
No PQ node: Remote LFA fails. TI-LFA crosses the gap
with an Adj-SID (A5).
Which way the tunnel leaves S
• PQ node in plain P(S): the tunnel follows S’s own
shortest path. It already avoids S–E.
• PQ node only in some P(N): the tunnel must go out
through N. S’s own path to it may use S–E.
Example 2: B → S’s own path S → A → B
C → exit via A
Why C needs the exit: S’s own path to C is S → E →
C, over the failed link. A’s path A → B → C avoids
it.
Several exits? Lowest c(S,N) + dist(N,PQ), then
lowest router id.
A neighbor with max metric 16,777,215 on its link is
never an exit (RFC 7490 §5.4).
Q-space looks towards E (B10)
P-space uses dist(S,Y): from S outwards. Q-space
uses dist(Y,E): from each router towards E.
With different metrics each way these differ, so
Q-space needs a reverse SPF rooted at E (A1).
Q-space aims for E, not D: once at E, the packet
follows E’s path to D. So one PQ node serves every
destination behind E (RFC 7490 §5.2.1.3).
RFC 7490 writes dist(S,E); it equals c(S,E) when S–E is
a primary link (D17).

Only when there is no LFA (B13)
Remote LFA is used only if (D, link S–E) has no LFA.
The P, Q and PQ sets are still shown in LFA Lab, for
learning.
Order: ECMP → LFA → Remote LFA → TI-LFA (B20).
What the tunnel is
RFC 7490 allows any tunnel. Older networks used an
LDP label over a targeted LDP session.
With Segment Routing it is just one more label: the
PQ node’s Prefix-SID (16004 for B).
Never in any set
S can’t pass its own tests, and E is never listed:
if E were in some P(N), N would already be an LFA
Extended P-space is on by default; untick it and PQ =
{B} here.
Takeaway
P-space = routers S reaches without the failed link; Q-space = routers that reach E without it. A router in both (a PQ node) is a safe place to tunnel to. Remote LFA
fixes most rings, but fails when P-space and Q-space don’t meet.
